headline: Bank Rate has been on hold at 3.75% since December 2025, but the 10-year gilt yield has jumped about 107bp since February to 5.36%, a headwind for office pricing.
summary: The Bank of England has held Bank Rate at 3.75% since December 2025, after cutting from 5.0% in October 2024. Long-term rates have moved the other way: the 10-year gilt par yield rose from 4.29% in February 2026 to 5.36% in early October, as CPIH re-accelerated from 2.8% (June) to 3.3% (August). Growth is modest but positive (GDP +0.5% q/q in Q2 2026), UK unemployment is 4.9% and London's employment rate is 74.8%.
insights: The 10-year gilt is at 5.36%, up from 4.29% in February 2026 and 4.41% in October 2024; month-end yields are the highest since at least October 2024.
The yield curve has steepened: the gilt-Bank Rate gap has widened from ~0.5pp to ~1.6pp, so long-term financing costs are rising even with policy rates on hold.
CPIH re-accelerated to 3.3% in August from 2.8% in June, reducing the chance of near-term rate cuts.
UK unemployment eased from 5.2% (late 2025) to 4.9%; GDP grew 0.6% in Q1 and 0.5% in Q2 2026.

signals.title: Rising gilt yields squeeze property yields
signals.rationale: A ~107bp rise in the 10-year gilt since February compresses the prime yield spread and pressures capital values unless rental growth compensates.

signals.title: Refinancing pressure for leveraged owners
signals.rationale: Higher long-term rates raise refinancing costs, which may force sales by over-leveraged owners.

signals.title: Distressed or motivated sellers
signals.rationale: Well-capitalised, long-term investors such as Nan Fung may find acquisition opportunities as financing stress rises.
